# Materials and methods {#sec-article-02-materials-methods}

## Study framework and data

The case study comprises the 311 zoning records used by the Congonhas project and their combined municipal footprint, approximately 304.07 km². The existing dispersion scenario includes a regional inventory and sources outside the municipal boundary. Modelled concentrations therefore represent received contributions from the included regional sources rather than only emissions assigned to Congonhas. Inventory year 2023 was applied to meteorological years 2021–2023; these are not three independently reconstructed annual inventories.

The monitoring network provides observations from seven PM~10~ stations and four PM~2.5~ stations. The previously developed monitoring–modelling integration is retained as a screening baseline. Its temporal coverage, spatial eligibility and benchmark comparisons are not replaced by the relative classes introduced here. Observed–modelled comparisons use overlapping periods where available, and the convention linking observation timestamps to the meteorological time base remains under documentary verification.

## Concentration indicators and spatial support

The analysis uses native annual AERMOD means averaged over the three model years and the mean of the three annual P98 indicators of daily concentrations. The daily model series was reconstructed from hourly POST output using an independent meteorological calendar and checked against native 24-hour output. The P98 treatment is a study indicator; it is not presented as the legal exceedance-counting rule for PM~10~. No percentile transformation was applied to reduce bias in the model–observation comparison.

Of 1,497 regional receptors, 1,008 fall within the combined zoning footprint. Their nearest-neighbour spacing has a median of 526.2 m, illustrating that the existing design is not a perfectly uniform 500 m lattice. Clipped Voronoi polygons provide a complete support partition for translating receptor attributes into area fractions. They are geometric accounting units, not evidence that concentrations are uniform inside each polygon. All numerical classification uses the original receptor values; cartographic interpolation does not create additional observations.

## Relative classes and concentration-profile groups

For each pollutant, annual concentrations were divided at the municipal receptor P20, P40, P60 and P80 values. Ties remain in the same class, so quintile labels need not produce equal counts when values coincide. These cutoffs are empirical properties of the selected domain and period. They do not define clean air, ambient saturation or legal thresholds.

Ward hierarchical clustering and k-means were compared for two to six groups using four features: annual and P98 concentrations for PM~10~ and PM~2.5~. The features were transformed with log(1+C) and standardized before fitting. K-means used ten seeded initializations, retaining the solution with the smallest within-group sum of squares. Mean silhouette quantified internal separation. No emission variable, zone identifier or geographic coordinate was included as a clustering feature. Groups can be spatially discontinuous; they are not automatically a set of contiguous control districts.

## Spatial association and sensitivity

Global and local Moran statistics were calculated for log(1+C). The reference weights assign equal weight to the eight nearest municipal neighbours and are row standardized. Global inference used 999 permutations. Local inference held the focal value fixed and sampled the remaining locations without replacement, producing two-sided conditional pseudo-p-values. Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment was applied separately to the local tests for each analysed field, using a nominal 5% false-discovery threshold (Anselin, 1995; Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995).

High–high and low–low indicate a location and its spatial lag above or below the standardized mean. High–low and low–high denote spatial contrasts. Non-significance is retained as a separate outcome and is not interpreted as low concentration. Local results were compared with four and twelve neighbours. Correlograms used successive 750 m distance bands up to 7.5 km, with 199 exploratory global permutations per band. Those bands describe distance dependence and do not relocate receptors.

Further sensitivity checks compared each year's quintile labels with the triennial labels. Alternative 500 m sampling origins were also evaluated by selecting the nearest existing receptor within 354 m of each target location. This is an analytical resampling experiment with explicit unsupported targets, not an AERMOD simulation at shifted coordinates. It assesses one component of sampling dependence while leaving the underlying concentration field unchanged.

## Emission allocation and associative thresholds

Annual source masses were allocated to the support polygons using the intersection fraction of area or length; point sources were assigned once. Source geometries, pollutant identifiers and annual masses came from the audited territorial emissions dataset. Volume-source footprints are acknowledged as geometric representations where a physical emitting area is not documented. Emission density was calculated per support-cell area, avoiding interpretation of a volume-source footprint as a measured surface emission density.

A complementary bivariate local Moran analysis related concentration at a receptor to emission density at neighbouring support units. It does not identify the responsible transport pathway or control for in-place correlation between emissions and concentrations. Accordingly, it is interpreted together with source-group output, not as a source–receptor model or evidence of causality.

Four increasing emission thresholds were fitted separately for the concentration P20, P40, P60 and P80 targets. For each binary target, a one-split classifier selected the emission cutoff maximizing balanced accuracy, with at least 5% of training cases on each side. Annual mass and support-cell emission density were tested separately. Whole 2 km and 4 km spatial blocks were assigned to five folds. The concentration targets were fixed properties of the reference field. Cutoff variation and test balanced accuracy were retained. Four finite, distinct and increasing cuts were required before creating five candidate emission intervals. These associations do not establish allowable emissions or causal concentration responses.

## Source attribution and zoning translation

Three-year annual source-group means were checked against the ALL output. Enterprise groups and Urban Total form the exclusive partition used in percentages. The exposed-area aggregate and urban subgroups were not added again. Group shares for high–high regions were calculated as ratios of area-weighted concentration contributions, rather than as shares of locally emitted mass. This distinction follows the separation between source attribution and control sensitivity discussed by Clappier et al. (2017).

Support polygons were intersected with zoning records. Each zone retains its shares of area in Q1–Q5 and in the local spatial classes, together with area-weighted annual concentration and group shares. This preserves internal heterogeneity. Touching support cells of the same significant high–high or low–low class were connected into regions, including corner contacts. An initial ABC contribution ranking was restricted to high–high regions, retaining the contribution that crosses each cumulative 80% and 95% boundary in the preceding class. Near-zero-area cadastral fragments remain identified in the output; a proximity support flag is used where numerical overlay is unstable. Their retention maintains record traceability and does not validate them as independently meaningful planning units.

## Planned exposure and emission-timing extensions

The dissertation extension will refine the residential support of census population before estimating the overlap between residents and concentration patterns. Existing sector totals alone do not locate every dwelling. Local health-event counts, compatible age groups and a verified concentration–response function are required to convert relative health fractions into numbers of events. Andreão et al. (2020) provides a Brazilian application relevant to this extension, and Chen and Hoek (2020) provides complementary evidence for reviewing long-term mortality functions. This manuscript reports no new estimate of avoided deaths.

Two candidate temporal emission scenarios were prepared for review, preserving mean daily emission factors while reducing hypothetical night-time road activity. They retain the current source geometry, inventory mass and meteorology. Their operating schedules are illustrative and have not been inferred as real from station concentration profiles. Existing hourly-emission sources remain excluded from an additional temporal multiplier. Improvement of model performance will require an actual rerun and evaluation on data not used to select the profiles.

## Wind-conditioned envelopes and management roles

Hourly ALL outputs were matched to valid non-calm hours in the actual AERMET surface file. Wind-from sectors of 45 degrees were centred on the eight main compass directions. The maximum concentration and its timestamp were retained at each receptor within each sector. These receptor-wise maxima form a non-simultaneous envelope, not a reconstructed dust cloud. Complete daily means were examined separately on days with at least 18 valid hours, circular resultant at least 0.5 and at least 50% of hours in the mean wind sector. These persistence choices are exploratory. The sector analysis complements the meteorological and surface-driver perspective discussed by Ribeiro et al. (2025), without transferring TSP thresholds to PM~10~ or PM~2.5~.

Four proposed management roles cover the analytical support. Receiving priority denotes annual concentration above P80. Source-control investigation denotes emission above the associative P80 cutoff without concentration in the top band. Lower relative impact requires concentration at or below P40 and emission at or below its corresponding associative cutoff. Other combinations remain under follow-up. Shared boundary segments, rather than corner contacts alone, connect cells into management regions. ABC was recalculated for the receiving-priority regions. The initial significant high–high ranking remains a separate sensitivity comparison. Brazil's Conama Resolution 513/2026 provides a national framework for air quality control regions, whereas these municipal roles are proposed analytical categories.

## Temporal identifiability before emission adjustment

Hourly group outputs were extracted at monitoring receptors and compared as normalized diurnal profiles. Geometric distances were retained as context, not inverse-distance attribution weights. Existing enterprise groups contain both static sources and sources already driven by HOUREMIS. Therefore, fitting a multiplier to an entire group would also alter its hourly-emission component. Auxiliary static-only groups were prepared for a future response-matrix run. A subsequent constrained inversion should use a limited, regularized set of temporal parameters, non-negative factors, documented activity priors, calendar-based mass conservation and withheld periods or stations. Vardag and Maiwald (2024) illustrates the relevance of network information and identifiability in an urban tracer inversion. Its quantitative results are not transferred to particulate matter.

## Complete-meteorology reference and paired directional maps

The directional analyses were evaluated against a complete-meteorology reference. Receptor-wise maxima of 1 h and 24 h were selected from all eligible periods in 2021-2023, without filtering by wind direction or hour of day. The long-term indicator remained the arithmetic mean of the three native annual means. Quintiles, local spatial association, emission-concentration screening, management regions and received contributions were evaluated separately for the six fields. An additional joint clustering used the three indicators for both pollutants after log(1+C) transformation and standardization. The earlier four-indicator analysis was retained as a distinct comparison rather than relabelled retrospectively.

Eight wind-origin sectors of 45 degrees were centred on N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W and NW. Paired figures show the two pollutants for the same sector and duration. Their directional icon identifies the selected origin sector, without encoding frequency or speed. Contributions to each short-term envelope were sampled at the event of ALL at the same receptor. Annual contributions use the same three native annual means. The envelopes are not simultaneous events across receptors or pollutants.
